summary.text: At \(n=5{,}319{,}426\), the odd number \(a(n)+4=59{,}496{,}778{,}573{,}193\) lies strictly between the two proposed endpoints.  It is Sierpiński because a covering of exponents modulo \(48\) gives a proper divisor of \((a(n)+4)2^m+1\) for every \(m>0\): respectively \(3,5,17,257\) on the classes \(m\equiv0\pmod2,\ 3\pmod4,\ 1\pmod8,\ 13\pmod{16}\), and \(97,673,7\) on the remaining classes \(m\equiv5,21,37\pmod{48}\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=9{,}454{,}129+11{,}184{,}810n.
\]
Recall that a Sierpiński number is an odd integer \(k>1\) such that, for every positive integer \(m\), the number
\[
k2^m+1
\]
is composite (equivalently, is not prime).

We disprove the conjecture by exhibiting one value of \(n\) for which another Sierpiński number lies strictly between \(a(n)\) and \(a(n)+28\).

Take
\[
n_0=5{,}319{,}426.
\]
Direct arithmetic gives
\[
11{,}184{,}810\cdot 5{,}319{,}426=59{,}496{,}769{,}119{,}060,
\]
and hence
\[
A:=a(n_0)=59{,}496{,}778{,}573{,}189.
\]
Define
\[
K=A+4=59{,}496{,}778{,}573{,}193.
\]
We will prove that \(K\) is a Sierpiński number. Since
\[
A<K=A+4<A+28,
\]
this will show that \(A\) and \(A+28\) are not consecutive Sierpiński numbers.

First, \(K\) is odd, because its last digit is \(3\), and clearly \(K>1\). It remains to prove that \(K2^m+1\) is not prime for every positive integer \(m\). In fact, the argument below works for every integer \(m\ge 0\).

We use a finite covering of the possible exponents. The following modular data are the key computations:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c}
p&o&r&K\pmod p&2^o\pmod p&2^r\pmod p\\ \hline
3&2&0&2&1&1\\
5&4&3&3&1&3\\
17&8&1&8&1&2\\
257&16&13&249&1&225\\
97&48&5&3&1&32\\
673&48&21&8&1&84\\
7&3&1&3&1&2
\end{array}
\]
For completeness, the last column in each row annihilates \(K2^r+1\) modulo the corresponding \(p\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
2\cdot1+1&=3\equiv0\pmod3,\\
3\cdot3+1&=10\equiv0\pmod5,\\
8\cdot2+1&=17\equiv0\pmod{17},\\
249\cdot225+1&=56{,}026=257\cdot218,\\
3\cdot32+1&=97,\\
8\cdot84+1&=673,\\
3\cdot2+1&=7.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus, in every row,
\[
K2^r+1\equiv0\pmod p.
\]
The period computations \(2^o\equiv1\pmod p\) are also direct. For the smaller moduli they include
\[
2^2=4\equiv1\pmod3,
\quad 2^4=16\equiv1\pmod5,
\quad 2^8=256\equiv1\pmod{17},
\]
\[
2^{16}=65{,}536\equiv1\pmod{257},
\quad 2^3=8\equiv1\pmod7,
\]
and direct repeated squaring gives \(2^{48}\equiv1\pmod{97}\) and \(2^{48}\equiv1\pmod{673}\). The displayed residues of \(K\) and of the indicated powers of \(2\) are ordinary integer remainder computations.

We now explain how these computations apply to arbitrary exponents. If
\[
2^o\equiv1\pmod p
\quad\text{and}\quad
m\equiv r\pmod o,
\]
then \(m=r+qo\) for some nonnegative integer \(q\), and therefore
\[
2^m=2^r(2^o)^q\equiv2^r\pmod p.
\]
Consequently, whenever one of the rows of the table applies,
\[
K2^m+1\equiv K2^r+1\equiv0\pmod p.
\]
So the corresponding \(p\) divides \(K2^m+1\).

It remains to show that the congruence classes attached to these seven rows cover every exponent. The cover can be written as follows:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{condition on }m&\text{divisor of }K2^m+1\\ \hline
m\equiv0\pmod2&3\\
m\equiv3\pmod4&5\\
m\equiv1\pmod8&17\\
m\equiv13\pmod{16}&257\\
m\equiv5\pmod{48}&97\\
m\equiv21\pmod{48}&673\\
m\equiv37\pmod{48}&7
\end{array}
\]
Here is a complete case analysis proving that this table is exhaustive.

If \(m\) is even, the first row applies. Suppose next that \(m\) is odd. If \(m\equiv3\pmod4\), the second row applies. Otherwise an odd integer must satisfy \(m\equiv1\pmod4\). If it is \(1\pmod8\), the third row applies. Otherwise it is \(5\pmod8\).

There are exactly six residue classes modulo \(48\) that are \(5\pmod8\), namely
\[
5,13,21,29,37,45\pmod{48}.
\]
Among these, the classes \(13,29,45\pmod{48}\) are all \(13\pmod{16}\), so the fourth row applies to them. The only remaining classes are
\[
5,21,37\pmod{48},
\]
which are handled by \(97,673,7\), respectively. In the final case, \(m\equiv37\pmod{48}\) implies \(m\equiv1\pmod3\), as required by the row with \(p=7,o=3,r=1\). This proves that every integer exponent belongs to at least one of the listed classes.

We can also spell out the divisibility in each case directly from the modular data:

* If \(m\) is even, then \(m\equiv0\pmod2\), so \(2^m\equiv1\pmod3\). Since \(K\equiv2\pmod3\),
  \[
  K2^m+1\equiv2\cdot1+1\equiv0\pmod3.
  \]

* If \(m\equiv3\pmod4\), then \(2^m\equiv2^3\equiv3\pmod5\). Since \(K\equiv3\pmod5\),
  \[
  K2^m+1\equiv3\cdot3+1\equiv0\pmod5.
  \]

* If \(m\equiv1\pmod8\), then \(2^m\equiv2\pmod{17}\). Since \(K\equiv8\pmod{17}\),
  \[
  K2^m+1\equiv8\cdot2+1\equiv0\pmod{17}.
  \]

* If \(m\equiv13\pmod{16}\), then \(2^m\equiv2^{13}\equiv225\pmod{257}\). Since \(K\equiv249\pmod{257}\),
  \[
  K2^m+1\equiv249\cdot225+1=56{,}026\equiv0\pmod{257}.
  \]

* If \(m\equiv5\pmod{48}\), then \(2^m\equiv2^5=32\pmod{97}\). Since \(K\equiv3\pmod{97}\),
  \[
  K2^m+1\equiv3\cdot32+1=97\equiv0\pmod{97}.
  \]

* If \(m\equiv21\pmod{48}\), then \(2^m\equiv2^{21}\equiv84\pmod{673}\). Since \(K\equiv8\pmod{673}\),
  \[
  K2^m+1\equiv8\cdot84+1=673\equiv0\pmod{673}.
  \]

* If \(m\equiv37\pmod{48}\), then \(m\equiv1\pmod3\), so \(2^m\equiv2\pmod7\). Since \(K\equiv3\pmod7\),
  \[
  K2^m+1\equiv3\cdot2+1=7\equiv0\pmod7.
  \]

Thus, for every \(m\ge0\), the number \(K2^m+1\) has a divisor in
\[
\{3,5,7,17,97,257,673\}.
\]
Every one of these divisors is greater than \(1\). It is also a proper divisor: since \(2^m\ge1\),
\[
K2^m+1\ge K+1>673,
\]
whereas every listed divisor is at most \(673\). Therefore \(K2^m+1\) has a divisor strictly between \(1\) and itself and hence is composite. In particular this holds for every positive \(m\).

We have proved that \(K=59{,}496{,}778{,}573{,}193\) is odd, greater than \(1\), and that \(K2^m+1\) is composite for every positive integer \(m\). Hence \(K\) is a Sierpiński number.

Finally,
\[
a(n_0)=59{,}496{,}778{,}573{,}189,
\qquad
a(n_0)+28=59{,}496{,}778{,}573{,}217,
\]
and
\[
a(n_0)<K=a(n_0)+4<a(n_0)+28.
\]
Thus a Sierpiński number lies strictly between the two claimed consecutive Sierpiński numbers at \(n_0=5{,}319{,}426\). Therefore the assertion that \(a(n)\) and \(a(n)+28\) are consecutive Sierpiński numbers for every \(n\ge0\) is false.
